newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FOCUS - Rouble Eurobonds promise but problems remain.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rouble Eurobonds promise but problems remain.

text.p: Russian plans to issue a rouble Eurobond next year, which would open a new sector in the Euromarkets, are not impossible, but many obstacles must first be cleared, bond analysts said on Friday.

Finance Minister Alexander Livshits, talking a day after the successful launch of Russia's first mark Eurobond, said Russia wanted to place rouble paper alongside its dollar and mark issues, describing a rouble Eurobond as his dream.
"I think it's a completely viable and promising option," said Dirk Damrau, managing director and head of research at Moscow investment bank Renaissance Capital.
But Damrau and other analysts said much work on the regulatory, taxation and legislation front was needed before rouble Eurobonds could be issued.
"It's like talking about going on a space flight before you've flown a plane," said one analyst at a Russian brokerage.
Livshits was clearly encouraged by Thursday's sizzling start of the two billion mark, seven-year issue, only Russia's second Eurobond, which was helped on its way by a nine percent coupon.
Investor interest in Russia was demonstrated last November, when its $1 billion debut offering -- the biggest ever sovereign debut Eurobond -- was massively oversubscribed.
At the same time foreign investors have shown they are hungry for domestic rouble paper.

Non-residents hold around $8 billion of Russian GKO Treasury bills and OFZ government bonds, according to the central bank, and possibly another $2 billion acquired outside the official scheme for foreign investment, Damrau said.
"A wide range of investors are comfortable with rouble risk at the moment," he said.
But Russia will need to make further progress on making the rouble fully convertible before rouble Eurobonds can be issued.

Russia has signed Article Eight of the International Monetary Fund on current account convertibility, and intends to dismantle restrictions on foreigners buying its T-bills and bonds and repatriating the proceeds by the end of the year.
Convertibility is a key issue, said Robert Devane, head of fixed income sales and trading at Moscow broker Troika Dialog.
"This is only practical if the rouble becomes a fully convertible, fungible currency," he said of a rouble Eurobond.
Euroclear, the clearing house for Eurobonds, will only accept them if their currency is convertible, he noted.
Russian legislation must be adapted to the needs of foreign bondholders, a lengthy process, and taxation issues clarified.

Russia recently imposed a 15 percent tax on earnings from new issues of T-bills. It has exempted the sovereign Eurobonds from this tax, but it is not clear whether planned regional Eurobonds are liable to it, and uncertainties about the scope of the tax disrupted T-bill issues at the start of the year.
Then the question arises who will buy a rouble Eurobond.
Damrau said foreigners now buying Russian T-bills, such as investment bank proprietary traders, hedge funds and emerging market funds would all be interested.
But Devane said a rouble Eurobond, settling in roubles, would be of most interest to domestic buyers.

There is certainly an appetite for Eurobonds in emerging currencies. Czech crown Eurobonds are no longer a rarity, and this week the World Bank and International Finance Corp issued Eurobonds in Philippine pesos.
A rouble contract planned by the Chicago Board of Trade will make it possible to hedge rouble Eurobonds, Devane said.
But in the end price will be the deciding factor.

Russia's recent fixed-rate three-year OFZ bond maturing June 1999 yields 24.5-25.0 percent in roubles, offering a dollar return to foreign investors of 13 percent. That compares with a yield on Russian dollar or mark Eurobonds of 9.0-9.5 percent.
"If Russia is willing to pay that sort of dollar yield for a Euro rouble issue, I'm sure it will find an audience," he said.
